doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Brooklyn family, Brooklyn Tech, NYU and Columbia
summary: Raph grew up in Brooklyn; his father conducted TV shows and played Dixieland trombone. He took up trombone at Brooklyn Tech, studied music education at NYU (1951-55) and later earned a master's.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: And you grew up in New York City?

A musical family. My father was a musician. He ended up — well he ended up out of work — but in his heyday he conducted the “Stop the Music” television show and he conducted “Name that Tune,” the original shows back in the ‘50s. And he played, in his day, when he was in his 20s he played trombone with Dixieland groups, including Phil Napoleon and some of those in New York City. So when it came time for me to take music, I took piano at age eight, and when I went into high school at age fourteen I went to Brooklyn Tech of all places, and in order to avoid the lunchroom lines which were enormous, I went down to the basement. There was a sign you could take music lessons and I ended up signing up for the trombone. So I started trombone in high school. And went to New York University, took music education, which in those days I felt, or we all felt, you know, those interested in my career were thinking that this would be a good thing to fall back on in case things didn’t work out musically.
Mid-50s actually, yeah. Well I went to NYU from ’51 to ’55. And things did work out so I managed to do fairly decently professionally. Ten years later, in ’65, I decided to go
back for a master’s so I went to Teacher’s College, Columbia, and I got a master’s in Music Education.
